title: Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia: clinical and microbiological epidemiology in a health area of Southern Spain

claims.text: S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, meningitis and bacteremia in children and adults.
claims.byte_quote: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, meningitis and bacteremia in children and adults

claims.text: Pneumococcal bacteremia incidence is 15-35 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
claims.byte_quote: The incidence of this kind of bacteremia is 15–35 cases per 100,000 inhabitants

claims.text: In this study the median annual incidence was 2.9 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
claims.byte_quote: In our study the median annual incidence was 2.9 cases/100,000 inhabitants

claims.text: Serotype 19A was the most frequent, followed by serotypes 1, 7F and 14.
claims.byte_quote: Serotype 19A was the most frequent, followed by serotypes 1, 7F and 14.

claims.text: Forty percent of bacteremias were caused by serotypes 19A, 1, 7F and 14.
claims.byte_quote: Forty percent of bacteremias were caused by serotypes 19A, 1, 7F and 14

claims.text: Main predisposing factors for pneumococcal bacteremia were smoking, antimicrobial/corticosteroid use, COPD, and HIV infection.
claims.byte_quote: The main predisposing factors observed were smoking, antimicrobial and/or corticosteroids administration, chronic pulmonary obstructive disease and HIV infection

claims.text: The leading predisposing factor for S. pneumoniae bacteremia was cigarette smoking (29.9%).
claims.byte_quote: The main predisposing factor for _S. pneumoniae_ bacteremia was cigarette smoking (29.9%)

claims.text: Seventy percent of patients had predisposing factors.
claims.byte_quote: Seventy percent of patients had predisposing factors

claims.text: Invasive pneumococcal disease most frequently infects children under 2 years, older adults (>65 years), and those with co-morbidities.
claims.byte_quote: Overall, invasive pneumococcal disease most frequently cause infection in children less than 2 years old, older adults (>65 years old) and individuals with co-morbidities

claims.text: Among isolates, 77.6% were penicillin-susceptible, 17.9% penicillin-intermediate, and 4.5% penicillin-resistant.
claims.byte_quote: 77.6% of the isolates were penicillin-susceptible, while 17.9% were penicillin-intermediate and only 4.5% of these isolates were penicillin-resistant.

claims.text: In Spain, invasive penicillin-nonsusceptible strains in the general population range from 19-45%.
claims.byte_quote: In our country, the percentage of invasive strains penicillin-nonsusceptible in the general population range from 19–45%

claims.text: The most common bacteremia source was the low respiratory tract (46 patients).
claims.byte_quote: The most common focus was the low respiratory tract recorded for 46 patients

claims.text: In one case the source of infection was the cerebrospinal fluid; the source was unknown in 20 episodes.
claims.byte_quote: The source of bacteremia was considered unknown in 20 episodes.
100% of episodes were from community-acquired origin.

claims.text: Mortality associated with the bacteremia was 6%.
claims.byte_quote: In our study, the mortality associated to bacteremia was 6%.

claims.text: Five variables were significantly associated with mortality: age >65, male sex, Caucasian race, critical/poor clinical condition, and septic shock.
claims.byte_quote: Five variables were significantly associated with mortality from _S. pneumoniae_ bacteremia: age >65 years, male sex, Caucasian race, clinical condition critical and poor and septic shock.

claims.text: Antibiotics tested for susceptibility were Penicillin G, Amoxicillin, Erythromycin, Chloramphenicol, Vancomycin, Cefotaxime and Tetracycline.
claims.byte_quote: Penicillin G, Amoxicillin, Erythromycin, Chloramphenicol, Vancomycin, Cefotaxime and Tetracycline were tested
